cards.q: What can an inductive proximity sensor detect?
options: Any solid object
Metal only
Liquids through a plastic wall
Anything that reflects light
cards.why: Its magnetic field is only disturbed by metal. Capacitive sensors see almost anything; photoelectric ones use light.

cards.q: An inductive sensor's rated distance is Sn = {sn} mm. Keeping to the assured distance (0.81 × Sn), how close must an aluminium target (factor 0.4) be, in mm?
cards.why: Both reductions apply: 81% for the assured distance, then the metal's correction factor.

cards.q: A PNP sensor is wired to a PLC input. Where must the input's common go?
options: To 0 V
To +24 V
To the sensor's brown wire
Nowhere: PNP inputs need no common
cards.why: PNP switches +24 V onto the input, so current flows through the input to its common at 0 V. NPN sensors need the common at +24 V.

cards.q: A temperature transmitter is ranged 0 to {span} °C, 4–20 mA. It sends {ma} mA. What temperature is that, in °C?
cards.why: 4 mA is 0% and 20 mA 100%, a 16 mA span: $\frac{mA - 4}{16}$ of the range.

cards.q: How is a 2-wire 4–20 mA transmitter powered?
options: From a separate 230 V mains supply
From its own internal battery
From a third wire carrying 24 V
From the loop, over its two wires
cards.why: The transmitter lives on the loop's 4 mA or more, and signals by how much more it lets flow. That is one reason the bottom of the range is 4 mA, not 0.

cards.q: A 24 V loop supply feeds a 2-wire transmitter that needs at least {vmin} V across it. What is the most resistance the rest of the loop can have, in ohms, at 20 mA?
cards.why: At full scale the loop must still leave the transmitter {vmin} V: the rest, 24 − {vmin} V, may be dropped across the input and cable at 20 mA.

cards.q: What is a PT100?
options: A thermocouple made of platinum
A thermostat that trips at 100 °C
A platinum RTD of 100 Ω at 0 °C
A sensor with a 100 ms response
cards.why: An RTD: its resistance rises with temperature, about 0.385 Ω per °C for platinum.

cards.q: A PT100's resistance is about $100(1 + 0.00385T)$ Ω. What is it at {t} °C, in ohms?
cards.why: 100 Ω at 0 °C, plus 0.385 Ω for each degree.

cards.q: Why are RTDs often connected with three wires rather than two?
options: To carry a separate power supply
To cancel the resistance of the leads
To connect a second, spare sensor
To make the cable mechanically stronger
cards.why: Lead resistance adds to the sensor's and reads as extra temperature. A third wire lets the input measure it and take it off.

cards.q: Why does a thermocouple input need cold-junction compensation?
options: It measures relative to the terminals' temperature
Thermocouples only work below 0 °C without compensation
To stop the thermocouple wires from freezing
To convert the signal into 4–20 mA
cards.why: The voltage depends on the difference between the hot junction and where the wires meet the terminals. The input measures its terminal temperature and adds it.

cards.q: What pressure does a {h} m column of water make at its base, in kPa? (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s²)
cards.why: $p = \rho g h$ in pascals; ÷ 1000 for kPa. About 10 kPa per metre of water.

cards.q: A pressure transmitter at the bottom of a tank reads {p} kPa. The liquid's density is {rho} kg/m³. How deep is the liquid, in metres?
cards.why: Rearrange $p = \rho g h$: $h = \frac{ p }{\rho g}$, with p in pascals. A lighter liquid reads less pressure for the same level.

cards.q: An orifice plate gives {q1} m³/h at a differential pressure of {dp1} mbar. What flow gives {dp2} mbar?
cards.why: Flow goes as the square root of the differential pressure: a quarter of the DP is half the flow.

cards.q: A load cell is rated 2 mV/V and excited at {ve} V. Its signal goes to an amplifier with a gain of {g}. What is the amplifier output at full load, in volts?
cards.why: mV/V means millivolts of output per volt of excitation, at full load: 2 mV × {ve} V, then × {g} for the amplifier, and ÷ 1000 to turn mV into volts.

cards.q: A {cap} kg load cell gives 20 mV at full load (2 mV/V at 10 V). It reads {mv} mV. What is the load, in kg?
cards.why: The output is proportional to load: {mv} mV is {mv}/20 of full scale.

cards.q: Why calibrate a weighing system with test weights instead of trusting the load cell's mV/V?
options: Datasheet figures are always wrong, whatever the cell
Test weights warm the load cell up to working temperature
The law forbids relying on a datasheet figure alone
Mounting and the structure change the output
cards.why: A known weight calibrates the whole chain (zero and span), including side loads, friction and several cells sharing the load.

cards.q: Match each ISA tag with what it is.
cards.why: The first letter is what is measured; the rest say what the device does.

cards.q: On a P&ID, what does the first letter of a tag like FIC-101 tell you?
options: The type of device: here, a field instrument
The plant area
The measured variable: here, flow
The signal type
cards.why: ISA 5.1: first letter the measured or initiating variable; the following letters the functions (I indicate, C control).

cards.q: On an ISA P&ID, what does a dashed line between instruments show?
options: A process pipe
An electrical signal
A pneumatic signal
A future connection
cards.why: Dashed: electrical signal. A line with pairs of short cross-strokes: pneumatic. Solid, heavier: process.

cards.q: An air-to-open (fail-closed) control valve loses its air supply. What does it do?
options: Closes
Opens
Stays where it was
Goes to half open
cards.why: The actuator's spring drives it to its safe position when the air goes. Choose fail-open or fail-closed from what is safe for the process.

cards.q: What does an equal-percentage valve characteristic mean?
options: Flow rises in direct proportion to the valve's travel
The valve opens fully at a small travel
Every valve in the plant is the same size
Equal travel steps change flow by equal percentages
cards.why: Small changes near closed, big near open. It suits loops where the pressure drop across the valve varies with flow.

cards.q: A valve has Kv = {kv}. Water flows through it with a pressure drop of {dp} bar. What is the flow, in m³/h?
cards.why: Kv is the flow of water in m³/h at 1 bar drop; flow rises with the square root of the drop.

cards.q: A transmitter's accuracy is ±{pc}% of span. Its range is 0 to {span} bar. What is that in bar?
cards.why: A percentage of span is the same number of bar everywhere in the range, so it matters most near the bottom.

cards.q: A 0 to {span} bar gauge reads {rd} bar when the reference is {ref} bar. What is its error, as a percentage of span (negative if it reads low)?
cards.why: Error = reading − true value; ÷ span × 100. Negative means it reads low.

cards.q: A measurement has two independent uncertainties, ±{a}% and ±{b}%. What is the combined uncertainty, root-sum-square, in %?
cards.why: Independent uncertainties add as squares: $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$, less than simply adding them.

cards.q: A signal's highest frequency is {f} Hz. By Nyquist, what must the sample rate exceed, in Hz?
cards.why: Sample at more than twice the highest frequency, and in practice well more.

cards.q: An ADC with {bits} bits covers 0 to {rng} V. What voltage is one step, in mV?
cards.why: $2^n$ steps across the range: range ÷ $2^n$.

cards.q: A {f} Hz signal is sampled at {fs} Hz, too slowly. At what frequency does it appear in the samples, in Hz?
cards.why: Between half the sample rate and the sample rate, a signal folds back to fs − f. An anti-aliasing filter before the ADC stops this.

cards.q: In a step test the controller output is stepped by {du}%. The process value settles {dpv}% higher. What is the process gain?
cards.why: Process gain = change in PV ÷ change in output, both in % of range.

cards.q: After a step, the process value starts to move {l} s later and reaches 63% of its change {t63} s after the step. What is the time constant, in seconds?
cards.why: First order plus dead time: the dead time is the delay before anything moves; the time constant is from then to 63%.

cards.q: Why is a long dead time, compared with the time constant, hard to control?
options: Dead time makes the process gain negative
It makes the control valve stick in place
The controller cannot see its effect until later
It only affects the display, not the loop
cards.why: Acting on old information, a fast controller overcorrects and oscillates; it has to be tuned slower.

cards.q: A closed-loop test gives an ultimate gain Ku = {ku}. By Ziegler–Nichols, what proportional gain does a PI controller use?
cards.why: Ziegler–Nichols PI: Kc = 0.45 Ku, Ti = Pu ÷ 1.2. It is aggressive: many people detune it.

cards.q: At the ultimate gain the loop oscillates with a period Pu = {pu} s. By Ziegler–Nichols, what integral time does a PI controller use, in seconds?
cards.why: Ziegler–Nichols PI: Ti = Pu ÷ 1.2.

cards.q: A process has gain {k}, time constant {tau} s and dead time {th} s. Lambda tuning with λ = {lam} s (the closed-loop time constant you choose) is used for a PI controller. What is its proportional gain Kc?
cards.why: Lambda tuning: Kc = τ ÷ (K(λ + θ)), and Ti is set equal to τ. λ is the closed-loop time constant you choose: larger is gentler.

cards.q: In cascade control, what does the outer (master) controller's output do?
options: Drives the valve directly
Sets the inner (slave) loop's setpoint
Switches the inner loop to manual
Records the alarm history
cards.why: The fast inner loop (say, flow) handles its own disturbances; the slow outer loop (say, temperature) only asks it for a value.

cards.q: A blending loop must make the additive {p}% of the total blend flow. The main (wild) flow is {q} m³/h. What additive flow setpoint, in m³/h?
cards.why: Additive ÷ (main + additive) = {p}%, so additive = main × {p} ÷ (100 − {p}). It is not simply {p}% of the main flow, because the blend includes the additive.

cards.q: What is split-range control?
options: One output drives two devices over parts of its range
Two controllers share the one control valve between them
A control loop that is on only half the time
A flow split between two pipes by hand
cards.why: For example, 0–50% opens the cooling valve and 50–100% the heating valve, so one temperature controller covers both.

cards.q: Put ISA-88's procedural levels in order, from the top.
cards.why: A procedure makes the batch; unit procedures run on one unit each; operations are the major steps; phases are the smallest tasks, such as dose or heat.

cards.q: In ISA-88, what is a phase?
options: A whole batch from its start to its end
One phase of the three-phase supply
A recipe's list of raw materials
The smallest step doing one process task
cards.why: Phases are the building blocks that recipes call up with parameters.

cards.q: How does a control recipe differ from a master recipe?
options: It is the template used for every batch
It is the copy kept by the regulator
It is the copy for one batch, with its records
It controls the valves but not the motors
cards.why: The master recipe is the template; each batch runs from its own control recipe, which becomes that batch's record.

cards.q: Under ISA-18.2, what must every alarm have?
options: A horn and a flashing light
A defined operator response
A priority of high
An entry on the P&ID
cards.why: An alarm needs someone to do something. If nobody needs to act, it is an event or a message, not an alarm.

cards.q: An operator gets {n} alarms in one {h}-hour shift. What is the average per 10 minutes?
cards.why: There are 6 ten-minute periods an hour. Guidance (EEMUA 191) suggests about 1 per 10 minutes is manageable for long periods.

cards.q: What is an alarm flood, and a common cure?
options: Over 10 in 10 minutes; suppress by cause
One alarm repeating all day; delete it
An alarm for high water level; fit a pump
Alarms sent to too many screens; use fewer
cards.why: In a flood the operator cannot keep up, so the important one gets lost. State-based suppression and rationalisation cut the consequential alarms.

cards.q: The forward path of a loop has two blocks in series with steady-state gains of {g1} and {g2}. The feedback path has a gain of {h}. What is the closed-loop gain?
cards.why: Blocks in series multiply: G = {g1} × {g2}. Closed loop with negative feedback: $\frac{G}{1 + GH}$.

cards.q: A forward path of gain {g} has unity negative feedback. What is the closed-loop gain?
cards.why: Closed loop: $\frac{G}{1 + GH}$, with H = 1 here. The higher G, the closer to 1.

cards.q: A proportional-only loop has an open-loop steady-state gain of {k}, unity feedback. After a step in setpoint, what steady-state error is left, as a percentage of the step?
cards.why: With no integral action the error settles at $\frac{1}{1 + K}$ of the step. Integral action removes it.

cards.q: A system's characteristic equation is $s^2 + 2\zeta\omega_n s + {{b}} = 0$. What is its natural frequency ωn, in rad/s?
cards.why: The constant term is $\omega_n^2$.

cards.q: What does critical damping (ζ = 1) give?
options: The greatest overshoot of all the damping cases
A steady, lasting oscillation at constant amplitude
An unstable, growing response that never settles
The fastest response with no overshoot
cards.why: Below 1 it overshoots and rings; above 1 it is slower than it need be.

cards.q: A second-order system has a damping ratio of {z}. What percentage overshoot does it give to a step?
cards.why: Overshoot = $100e^{-\zeta\pi/\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}}$ per cent. ζ = 0.5 gives about 16%; 0.7 about 5%.

cards.q: What is a gain of {g} in decibels?
cards.why: Gain in dB = 20 log₁₀(gain). 10 is 20 dB, 0.1 is −20 dB, 2 is about 6 dB.

cards.q: Above the corner frequency of a first-order lag, how does its gain fall?
options: At 40 dB per decade
It stays flat
At 20 dB per decade
At 6 dB per decade
cards.why: Each tenfold rise in frequency cuts the gain tenfold (−20 dB); the phase heads to −90°. (20 dB per decade is 6 dB per octave.)

cards.q: A first-order lag has a time constant of {tau} s. What is its corner frequency, in Hz?
cards.why: Corner at $\omega = \frac{1}{\tau}$ rad/s, which is $\frac{1}{2\pi\tau}$ Hz.

cards.q: Where the loop's phase reaches −180°, its gain is {g}. What is the gain margin, in dB?
cards.why: Gain margin: how much the gain could rise before reaching 1 (0 dB) at −180°. 0.5 is about 6 dB.

cards.q: What is a loop's phase margin?
options: The phase at the lowest frequency
The phase above −180° where the gain is 1
The difference between two setpoints
The loop's time delay, in degrees
cards.why: Around 45° to 60° gives a well-damped response; near 0° the loop rings and is close to instability.

cards.q: Where must a closed loop's poles be for it to be stable?
options: All in the left half of the s-plane
All on the imaginary axis
All in the right half
Anywhere, as long as there are two
cards.why: Poles with negative real parts give responses that die away; a pole in the right half grows without limit.

cards.q: A loop's closed-loop time constant is {tau} s. By the usual rule of thumb for samples per time constant, what is the longest sample time, in seconds?
cards.why: Sample at least ten times per time constant, so the digital loop behaves almost like a continuous one.

cards.q: A digital PI controller integrates its error on every scan. With Ki = {ki} per second, error {e}% and Ts = {ts} s, how much does it add to its integral each scan, in %?
cards.why: The integral is a running total: each scan adds Ki × error × scan time, $K_i \times e \times T_s$.

cards.q: Why does a slow sample time hurt a control loop?
options: It raises the gain of the process
It removes the integral action
It only makes the trend look rough
It adds delay, which eats phase margin
cards.why: The controller acts on values up to a sample old, and holds its output between samples: both are delay, and delay costs phase.
